{"id": "2:282/q83", "question": "What interpretive methods do the cited works discuss?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different readings, referents, grounds, or applications.", "positions": [{"id": "2:282/q83/p1", "position": "YKHULI-TAJDID supplies interpretation context (c2).", "reasons": "YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī’s approach to Qur’anic interpretation lies at the intersection of preserving intellectual origins and renewing them. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Although modern historical, archaeological, and anthropological research recovered ancient national origins, consciousness had already settled within the Qur’anic frame. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an became the center around which the heritage sciences arose, beginning with the linguistic disciplines because the Qur’an is a linguistic phenomenon. YKHULI-TAJDID (حسن حنفي): Ḥasan Ḥanafī contrasts an Islamic civilization formed around the Qur’an with Western Christian civilization, where the book emerged from tradition; the Gospels followed the Christian call rather than serving as its source. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author notes that seventeenth-century historical criticism, associated with Spinoza, Richard Simon, and Jean Astruc, examined alteration and change in sacred books. YKHULI-TAJDID (حسن حنفي): Ḥasan Ḥanafī identifies three distinguishing Qur’anic features: it is the final, complete revelation; preserved in writing; and revealed gradually over twenty-three years in response to human needs. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author links gradual, situation-responsive revelation to Al-Khūlī’s principle that the Qur’an is closely connected to human life, which grounds his literary school of interpretation. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī’s literary approach challenges rigid, literal, static exegesis because that mode permits neither development nor renewal. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretation is the starting point for intellectual work that renews the civilization, because the Qur’an anchors its origins and Muslim communal identity. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Al-Khūlī uses the psychological dimension to connect religion and literature and argues for reading the Qur’an topic by topic. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Topical interpretation is always colored by the historical period in which it is undertaken. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an uses taʾwīl, while legal theorists developed a specialized sense that later became common among theologians; Al-Khūlī considers tafsīr broader than taʾwīl. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretive forms multiply because interpreters bring different cultural backgrounds to the text. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics has an older sense, the interpretation of sacred books, and a modern sense that developed into a major late-twentieth-century philosophical current. YKHULI-TAJDID (فيلهلم دلتاي): Dilthey’s hermeneutic position treats interpretation or understanding as a method for the social and historical sciences. YKHULI-TAJDID (مارتن هيدجر): Heidegger’s position treats interpretation as an ontological, existential event in which text and interpreter interact within the history of understanding. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author follows the Heideggerian line, treating hermeneutics as lived experience of texts and as dialogue that fuses text and reader across past and present. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics applies to religious, inherited, philosophical, and legal texts; in reading, text and reader, past and present, enter a reciprocal relation that keeps new understanding possible. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): A text gains particular content when a present-day reader speaks on its behalf; without the present’s participation, it becomes frozen and detached from reality. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): A writer’s work of classification ends when the text is produced, but reading, interpretation, and understanding remain open-ended tasks. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics became an independent discipline that both draws on and informs the human sciences; it engages theories of knowledge, being, and value, especially epistemology. YKHULI-TAJDID (هانز جيورج جادامر): Gadamer’s Truth and Method (1960) established hermeneutics as a powerful method, said to rival experimental science in importance for understanding the human reality of texts. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics developed schools and became a broad intellectual current with strong influence on cultural life and literary criticism. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author compares the Qur’an’s appearance in Arab civilization to philosophy’s appearance in the West: each was a decisive turn in outlook and method. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Hermeneutics rejects the gap between reader and text: meaning depends on the context of production and the recipient’s horizon, so it varies across times and places. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Interpretation makes the text living and renewable by placing responsibility on reading: the reader reshapes its raw material according to the cultural horizon of the present. YKHULI-TAJDID (أمين الخولي): Al-Khūlī argues that a reader’s personality, intellectual level, and mental horizon limit what the reader can understand from a text; Arabic’s rich resources permit many interpretive extensions. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author attributes the crisis of Islamic culture and Arab civilization to the failure of interpretation and renewal, followed by a long era of commentaries, glosses, and marginalia. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Renewing Qur’anic interpretation is necessary for the renewal and flourishing of Arab-Islamic thought, a goal pursued by Islamic thinkers since the Nahḍa began. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The author concludes that Al-Khūlī substantially achieved this renewalist aim. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Pre-revelation cultural inheritances persisted in Egypt through Pharaonic customs and the Coptic calendar, and other Muslim countries also retained pre-Qur’anic inheritances. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Despite those inheritances, the Qur’an quickly gathered them into a new civilizational phase that shaped the later historical course. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an’s linguistic character makes authenticity a distinctive concern: language is the fabric of thought and consciousness, not a container for thought. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): The Qur’an’s linguistic force accompanied a kind of historical amnesia, as conquered peoples abandoned their national languages, which had embodied earlier social life and values. YKHULI-TAJDID (author): Islam presented itself as a continuation, development, and refinement of earlier revealed religions, especially Judaism and Christianity."}, {"id": "2:282/q83/p2", "position": "RIFAI-KHULI supplies interpretation context (c2).", "reasons": "RIFAI-KHULI (author): Classical tajdīd meant reviving neglected religious practice in its original form; Khuli instead defines renewal as development that discovers something new through ijtihād. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author reads this account as showing Arabic's inherited Bedouin worldview and limited urban vocabulary; Abbasid Arabic then borrowed and coined terms to cover city life's new realities. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli held that developing beliefs is possible and now necessary, both because life requires it and to protect religion's continued relevance and compatibility with thought and action. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He urged a new approach to unseen matters, rejecting excessive attribution of phenomena to the unseen and detailed speculation that scientific-minded younger generations cannot absorb. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli opposed ahistorical readings of heritage: each tradition is shaped by the particular temporal and spatial conditions of its period and changes as those conditions change. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): He applied gradual progression to material and immaterial life alike: forms begin simply, compete, and develop as what is fit survives and becomes more complex. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli described Islamic beliefs as developing from simple early forms to more complex ones as Muslims moved from Bedouin life into civilization and encountered learning and other peoples' thought; he contrasted the clear creed of the salaf with the interpretive creed of later scholars. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Khuli departed from the revivalist reform program associated with al-Tahtawi, al-Afghani, and Muhammad Abduh, which relied on inherited principles to restore earlier glory. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author regards Khuli's position as an early call for a new kalām: an age-responsive effort to interpret and justify belief, protecting faith from extremism and stagnation as well as defending it. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author interprets Khuli's historicity as the view that ideas resemble and arise from their environments: intellectually fertile settings generate complex thought, while poorer settings produce simpler ideas. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli insisted that renewal begins by thoroughly understanding the old and changing our role from guarding and sanctifying heritage to studying it critically. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author reads Khuli's 'killing' of the old as discernment, not destruction: identify inert inherited elements and understand how their concepts and questions restrict present life and future movement. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli allowed renewal to find new insight by drawing on existing old material, as well as by independent reasoning that produces something previously unknown. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author says Khuli sought to breathe new

RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli made evolution comprehensive across fundamentals, beliefs, worship, and transactions, extending reform beyond the commonly accepted scope of legal dealings; the author says including worship may be his distinctive position. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author notes that worship is conventionally treated as fixed by revelation, unlike transactions, but Khuli still urged reconsidering legal and theological works in light of changing realities. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli argued that new events absent from old fiqh books cannot halt the world's course; rigidity risks alienating ordinary people from a religion unable to address their lives. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli fashioned a different path for understanding religion and interpreting its texts, beyond inherited foundations and principles. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): In a discussion with the Shaykh al-Azhar, Khuli rejected restricting change to a few worship rulings and said Islamic law selects what is easier to practice and best suited to endure. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli raised whether worshippers could follow congregational Friday and festival prayers through televised broadcasts, seeing and hearing the imam when local mosques are crowded. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): For Khuli, transactions turn on public benefit wherever it exists; evolving the presentation of beliefs, worship, and transactions should keep religious life connected to ordinary life. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author says Khuli did not fully explain the basis or applications of evolving worship rulings and cautiously reads him as seeking easier performance of obligations through a broader use of hardship relief and secondary rulings. RIFAI-KHULI (author): The author judges general calls to adapt fiqh insufficient unless scholars rebuild the underlying principles and inference rules so they can yield alternative rulings responsive to changing times and places. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai stresses that even Qur'an-by-Qur'an exegesis is shaped by hidden assumptions when an interpreter chooses one verse or word to explain another. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai says Khuli's position does not entail relativism; it frees Qur'anic meaning from exegetes' errors and treats their readings as historically conditioned rather than eternally authoritative. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai says Muhammad Ahmad Khalaf Allah embodied Khuli's reformist method, while Aisha Abd al-Rahman remained attached to inherited tafsir and did not adopt modern hermeneutics. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai suggests Bint al-Shati avoided departing from inherited methods out of fear after Khalaf Allah's dissertation drew fierce attacks; he adds that she may not have grasped Khuli's critique of inherited tafsir. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai argues that reform is emotionally and materially costly and requires courage to challenge convention. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai cites Muhammad Rashid Rida's Salafi turn after Muhammad Abduh's death as another example of students reverting to inherited tradition rather than following a reformist teacher. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli says interpreters color a text, especially a literary one: a reader's personality sets its intellectual level and the horizon within which its meaning is understood. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli describes readers as pulling a phrase in different directions and drawing from it only what their intellectual capacity permits; language's figurative range enables this coloring. RIFAI-KHULI (author): Al-Rifai suspects Khuli borrowed the image of coloring text from Junayd's saying that water takes its vessel's color, and sees Sufi and gnostic methods as valuable resources beyond inherited tafsir and legal theory. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli holds that interpreters' personalities mark every method and era of exegesis, whether transmitted or reasoned, despite claims of detachment and objectivity. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): Khuli rejects the claim that transmitted exegesis escapes the interpreter's personal imprint simply because it explains verses through reports without overt intervention. RIFAI-KHULI (أمين الخولي): For Khuli, a narrator's choice to gather reports that seem relevant to a verse, and to accept or reject them, exposes the interpreter's horizon and prior assumptions.
